arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. cma:136285.texto:
The monk-painter Sesshū is revered today, as he was in his own time. While he left Kyoto's sophisticated intellectual and cultural environment to live in a provincial village in a far western province, he seems never to have severed contacts with the monastic communities of his young adulthood. His residence in Yamaguchi proved fortuitous because his patron, the region's military lord, enjoyed considerable freedom in conducting trade missions overseas with Korea and China. Sesshū went to China in 1467 and traveled about the country, visiting well-known historical sites and Chan (Zen) temples before returning two years later. Thus he became familiar with contemporary painting practices, materials, formats, and subject matter. His assimilation and then transmission of these elements had a profound impact on the following generations of ink painters, patrons, and Zen communities throughout Japan. 

Despite the presence on these byōbu of the name "Sesshū," they are from the hand of another accomplished but as yet anonymous follower active in the middle of the sixteenth century. Sesshū's name here, as on a handful of similar bird-and-flower byōbu, attests to the master's identification at that time with the colorful mural paintings on the same theme emanating from Ming dynasty China. This genre had heretofore been relegated to hanging scroll compositions, so the intro-duction into temple and daimyo residences of such an attractive theme surely caused considerable excitement in the later fifteenth century, when in all likelihood Sesshū introduced it into the Japanese painting repertoire. Subsequently, artists of varying backgrounds and training tried their hands at these large, dramatic scenes. 

From right to left the composition portrays an array of flowering plants in the near distance that indicate the passage of the seasons. Birds, usually paired, occupy this setting, engaged in various activities that lend naturalism and an air of peacefulness. The world they inhabit may be characterized pictorially by expansive middle-ground waterscapes that end where the far distant mountains rise as backdrops. These features appear consistently in other bird-and-flower byōbu attributed to Sesshū. Also noteworthy is the absence of any birds of prey such as the samurai's beloved hawks, emblems of fierceness and graceful strength that appear often in the byōbu of sixteenth-century Kano and Soga school painters.
cma:136285.title: Birds and Flowers in a Landscape of the Four Seasons

cma:148357.texto:
East Asian paintings from China, Korea, and Japan were frequently conceived as sets of multiple images. These sets might have been composed for specific palace or temple rooms, or to portray a specific theme, such as the four seasons. Over time, the original intent of such sets is often lost through damage, changes in ownership, or a variety of other reasons. 

The identity of the artist can also be lost, but then, sometimes, retrieved. This pair of ink paintings has traditionally been labeled as Japanese and attributed to the 16th-century painter Genga. Since there are no seals or signature of the artist on the painting, this attribution was based on comparisons of brush style with paintings known to be by Genga. More recent study indicates that while the 16th century is an appropriate time frame for the pair, the precise cultural identity of the artist is not certain after all. The dark, eccentric shapes of the rocks and bamboo clusters and the dramatic tonal contrasts evident throughout the composition point to either Korean authorship or influence upon a Japanese painter of the period.
cma:148357.title: Bamboo in Rain; Bamboo in Wind

cma:159756.texto: Muromachi period (1392–1573) artists in Japan were keenly interested in Korean and Chinese culture. Paintings from the continent were avidly collected, studied, and copied for specific techniques and effects. Most painters, however, never had the opportunity to actually travel abroad. This painting presents a typical, idealized image of a Chinese scholar's retreat in the countryside. The misty background, however, brings a decidedly Japanese element to the composition. Japanese painters had long been interested in portraying the seasons and in suggesting the special atmosphere of a place.
cma:159756.title: Thatched Hut by Water's Edge

cma:170476.texto:
These screens present the cycle of the farming year, starting with spring at right and ending with fall at left. Close examination of these screens reveals moments of games and amusement, the enjoyment of meals as well as intellectual and spiritual pursuits interspersed among the scenes of cultivating and preparing the rice harvest.

The artist Kō Sūkoku is considered the 18th-century heir in style and attitude to Hanabusa Itchō (1652–1724). Itchō’s work incorporated elements from Kano school, ukiyo-e, and literati styles of painting. Kō trained with one of Hanabusa’s pupils, Sawaki Sūshi, who was best known for scenes depicting everyday life and customs.
cma:170476.title: Spring and Autumn Farming (Autumn)

afirmaciones.texto: Esta pintura japonesa presenta una imagen idealizada de un retiro campestre chino, pero incorpora un elemento japonés en el fondo brumoso, mostrando un interés japonés en las estaciones y la atmósfera del lugar.
La obra es un paisaje que combina influencias chinas con una sensibilidad japonesa, lo que la hace una interpretación japonesa de un paisaje similar al que podría encontrarse en China.
La obra es una pintura japonesa del siglo XVIII que representa escenas del ciclo agrícola, incluyendo actividades cotidianas y espirituales en el campo.
Aunque es un paisaje, se enfoca en la vida agrícola y social más que en un paisaje natural puro, por lo que no es el mismo tipo de paisaje que la imagen original.
Esta pintura japonesa del siglo XIX sigue la tradición de la escuela del Sur, que enfatiza el uso de tinta monocroma y pinceladas caligráficas.
Es un paisaje japonés que, aunque estilizado y con técnicas específicas, representa un paisaje natural, lo que puede relacionarse con el pedido de un paisaje pintado en Japón.
Esta obra japonesa del siglo XVI es un biombo con escenas de aves y flores en un paisaje que representa las cuatro estaciones, con influencia china y japonesa.
El paisaje incluye elementos naturales y atmosféricos que podrían relacionarse con un paisaje similar al de la imagen original, pero con un enfoque en flora y fauna.
Esta pareja de pinturas japonesas del siglo XVI, atribuidas a Genga, muestra bambú y rocas con influencias coreanas o de un pintor japonés influenciado por Corea.
Aunque no es un paisaje amplio como el de la imagen original, representa elementos naturales en un estilo japonés con influencias regionales.

plan.nota_de_identidad: Clase **1 / 2** (la tabla de identidades), el **híbrido**: se *direcciona* como caché de entradas —eso **es** el reuso del plan al barrer el peso de fusión, cinco corridas de un barrido de `α` reusando un plan— y su contenido es la salida **no determinista** de un LLM. Por eso la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica y lo que rige es **escritura única** (la escritura única del plan). lo que no entra en la identidad del plan: `α`, N, la fusión y el `variante_id` **no** son ingredientes. la versión del prompt como ingrediente del plan: el prompt **+ su versión**, el modelo y el muestreo **sí**.
plan.nota_de_pl3: Las **tres** cláusulas van escritas porque son **tres cosas**: que las dos consultas existan, que difieran del pedido crudo (*rewriting*) y que difieran entre sí (lo que distingue *expansion* de *rewriting*). El veredicto viaja adentro para que las tres cláusulas de las consultas del plan se pueda contar **también sobre una ad-hoc**, cuyo pedido el registro de decisiones no deja guardar.
plan.nota_de_pl5: la escritura única del plan: un `plan_id` se escribe **una sola vez**; si ya existe se **lee** y la corrida registra si lo **produjo o lo reusó**. Sin ese registro no habría forma de saber **qué corrida pagó la llamada que la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura cuenta**.

formato.nota: El formato concreto **sigue abierto**: esto es la **cosmética declarada**, no el contrato. El contrato —`[n]` que asigna el renderizador, toda afirmación con dato citando un `fragment_id` recuperado en esta consulta, 100 % de los CC-BY con atribución, español + cita textual en inglés— vive en el código y es el conteo de referencias colgadas, el criterio de atribución, el criterio de idioma y las obligaciones de la cita.

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. La cita viaja desde `knowledge` hasta acá **sin pasar por el modelo** (el contrato de salida), y las obligaciones de la cita lo verifica byte a byte: si el formateo viviera dentro del prompt, *'textual'* dependería de que el modelo no lo reescriba.

From right to left the composition portrays an array of flowering plants in the near distance that indicate the passage of the seasons. Birds, usually paired, occupy this setting, engaged in various activities that lend naturalism and an air of peacefulness. The world they inhabit may be characterized pictorially by expansive middle-ground waterscapes that end where the far distant mountains rise as backdrops. These features appear consistently in other bird-and-flower byōbu attributed to Sesshū. Also noteworthy is the absence of any birds of prey such as the samurai's beloved hawks, emblems of fierceness and graceful strength that appear often in the byōbu of sixteenth-century Kano and Soga school painters.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1960.173 · CC0 1.0

5. **Bamboo in Rain; Bamboo in Wind**
   Genga · early 1500s · hanging scroll; ink on silk
   Ficha oficial: https://clevelandart.org/art/1975.71

   Esta pareja de pinturas japonesas del siglo XVI, atribuidas a Genga, muestra bambú y rocas con influencias coreanas o de un pintor japonés influenciado por Corea. [1]
   Aunque no es un paisaje amplio como el de la imagen original, representa elementos naturales en un estilo japonés con influencias regionales.

   **Fuentes**
   [1] “East Asian paintings from China, Korea, and Japan were frequently conceived as sets of multiple images. These sets might have been composed for specific palace or temple rooms, or to portray a specific theme, such as the four seasons. Over time, the original intent of such sets is often lost through damage, changes in ownership, or a variety of other reasons. 

The identity of the artist can also be lost, but then, sometimes, retrieved. This pair of ink paintings has traditionally been labeled as Japanese and attributed to the 16th-century painter Genga. Since there are no seals or signature of the artist on the painting, this attribution was based on comparisons of brush style with paintings known to be by Genga. More recent study indicates that while the 16th century is an appropriate time frame for the pair, the precise cultural identity of the artist is not certain after all. The dark, eccentric shapes of the rocks and bamboo clusters and the dramatic tonal contrasts evident throughout the composition point to either Korean authorship or influence upon a Japanese painter of the period.”
       https://clevelandart.org/art/1975.71 · CC0 1.0
